name: Papa (पापा), 56

voice.register: Measured, even and quiet; never raised and never an exclamation mark (chapter 1's one shout is Mausi's). He talks like a platform announcement: an ordered run of whole sentences, each three to eight words with its verb and its full stop, one fact to a sentence, given one after another across one to three bubbles, and the last one names what comes next ('Ab checker aayega.'). That is his long shape, and it is unlike the other three long talkers: Mama ji trails on with commas and 'aur haan', Mausi triples and overlaps, Masterji gives a verdict and wanders into cloth and weather; Papa closes each sentence before he starts the next. Slow and exact. His only verbless lines are the time correction ('9:40, aaspaas nahin.') and the time stamp that opens his thanks. With Nani, who lets him finish, the run is longest (three bubbles); with everyone else it is usually two sentences. Numbers: one of the two people in the cast who lean on them (with Tinku), and only minutes, clock times and the count before a noun; never prices, scores or ordinals. Budget: at most one figure a bubble, and at least one bubble in three with none (in the test set below, 5 lines of 12 carry a figure). Humour is deadpan, about himself and clocks, delivered in the same flat announcement voice.
voice.mix: Careful standard Hindi of the railway colonies, belonging to no one town: full verbs, -इए to elders, no regional colour. English only for railway nouns every Indian traveller knows (coach, berth, platform, PNR, chart, waiting list, booking, ticket, running status, checker) and for clock times, which stay figures in all three modes ('9:40'). His verbs stay Hindi, many of them the railway's own (gaadi lagna, chhootna, chalna, chart banna, berth milna); he never builds a verb from an English word plus kar or ho, which is now Mummy's frame alone. So his praise is 'Sab confirm hai.' (the railway status word) instead of 'Confirm ho gaya.', and his thanks is 'Darj hai.' (entered, the parcel register's word) instead of 'Noted.' or 'note kar liya'. He switches by single nouns, as older speakers do in the Dehradun study the realism notes cite, never by whole English clauses (Mama ji and Mami do that). Tamil only in the coach count under his breath, kept in Tamil in every mode (a Tamil reader signs off the words and the script). When cross the English goes altogether: 'late' becomes 'der', 'halt' goes, and only the minutes stay. His typed messages are English (see typing); in English mode his spoken 'Darj hai.' is 'Noted.'
tics: Announces in order: whole sentences, one fact each, each closed with a full stop, the last naming the next step with 'ab ... aayega' | 'अब ... आएगा' | '... comes next' ('Ab checker aayega.' | 'The ticket checker comes next.'). He names the next item before anyone answers.
Corrects any vague time to the minute: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, not "around".' He hears 'about', 'around' and 'lagbhag' as errors; quoting the word back is the only time he says it.
The count before the thing: 'Hum solah log hain.' | 'Four trains this year.' (his alone: Tinku and Mama ji drop number-first).
Names a train by its time: '9:40 wali', '8:15 wali' ('the 9:40'), as railway people do.
Gives the minutes where others give feelings: two hours late is '120 minute'; good news is the minute it came ('Khabar 11:52 par aayi.').

Deadpan jokes in the station loudspeaker's frame: 'Kripya dhyan dein.' | 'Attention, please.' then a home fact ('Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.'). At most once a chapter, never while he asks (rule 37), all of it waiting on rulebook Q5.
Never describes a person's temperament; he logs what they did, with the minute.
Counts the coaches under his breath in Tamil as a train comes in: '...naalu, anju, aaru.' (a whisper bubble; proposal, a Tamil reader signs off).
Looks up for a clock before he speaks in any new place (a gesture in the panel, not a word).
When cross: the minutes left, then one word said twice ('Koi neeche na utre. Koi nahin.'), the guard's flat hand lowered palm down; quieter, never louder, and the English goes.

His judging notes on cards: one time stamp, then the act, in the Hindi transitive past so a note reads the same of a woman or a man; no ordinal and no second figure: '10:20. Asked the coach number again.' | '10:20। फिर से डिब्बे का नंबर पूछा।'; '11:55. Changed seats again.' | '11:55। फिर सीट बदली।'; '1:40. Woke everyone for tea.' | '1:40। चाय के लिए सबको जगाया।'; '12:10. Repacked the bag again.' | '12:10। फिर से बैग बाँधा।'; '9:50. Finished all the snacks.' | '9:50। सारा नाश्ता ख़त्म किया।'; '10:00 onwards. Hummed the same tune.' | '10:00 से। वही धुन गुनगुनाई।'. Never on a decision whose task the note bears on (rule 20), as often on women as on men, lengths kept even within a decision (story_take.length_faults).
catchphrases: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, आसपास नहीं।' | '9:40, not "around".' (the correction; his one catchphrase with a number in it, said whenever anyone gives a time with 'around' or 'about' in it; it replaces '9:40, not 9:45.', which held two figures; the owner may keep the old line as a marked exception)
'Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai.' | 'नहीं। चार्ट बन चुका है।' | 'No. The chart is made.' (his final no: once the railway chart is made, nothing changes)

'Dal ghadi dekhkar nahin banti. / Swaad se banti hai.' | 'दाल घड़ी देखकर नहीं बनती। / स्वाद से बनती है।' | 'Dal is not made by the clock. / It is made by taste.' (when anyone asks how long the dal takes: the one thing he will not time)
voice.exclamation: 'Kamaal hai.' | 'कमाल है।' | English mode 'Remarkable.' New. Said flat, with a full stop and never an exclamation mark, a whole sentence that keeps its verb. Two uses: real surprise at good news ('Kamaal hai. Khabar 11:52 par aayi.') and dry irony ('Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat bana? Kamaal hai.', the power cut that came on time). No religious meaning: 'kamaal' is an everyday word for a wonder or a feat. His alone: Mama ji's 'Kamaal!' goes (matrix 2.15). The English rendering avoids every mild word that hides a holy name (Gosh, Goodness, Good grief).
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: he corrects the record against himself, as a fact, the time first, then the right fact: '9:40 mera time tha. / Galat nikla. / Board par 9:25 hai.' | '9:40 मेरा टाइम था। / ग़लत निकला। / बोर्ड पर 9:25 है।' | '9:40 was my time. / It was wrong. / The board says 9:25.' Never 'sorry' (Mausi's alone), never 'Galti hui' (Mausa ji's), never 'Maaf kijiye' (yours). THANKS: he logs the deed with its minute, then 'Darj hai.' (it is entered): 'Mummy ji, 5:52 par chai seedhi par thi. / Darj hai.' | 'मम्मी जी, 5:52 पर चाय सीढ़ी पर थी। / दर्ज है।' | 'Mummy ji, the tea was on the step at 5:52. / Noted.' When he is thanked, the same word and then the next job: 'Darj hai. Ab wapsi ka ticket aayega.' | 'Noted. The return tickets come next.' The family knows 'Darj hai.' is his thank-you. LOVE: never said in words. A deed done ahead of time, announced as a plain fact ('Didi, neeche ki berth aapki hai. / March mein hi ho gayi thi.'); 'Reached?' typed after any journey you make without him (his alone); standing on the platform till the last coach has gone ('Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.'), the colony-gate boy grown up. The nearest he comes to pride is the album's count: 'Four trains this year. / Nobody ever had to remind you.'
uses: Clock times in figures, to the minute: 9:40, 6:35, 5:52, 8:55; minutes for any delay ('120 minute')
ab ... aayega | अब ... आएगा | ... comes next
Sab confirm hai | सब कन्फ़र्म है | It is all confirmed (his highest praise)
Darj hai | दर्ज है | Noted (his thanks, and his answer to being thanked)
Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai | नहीं। चार्ट बन चुका है | No. The chart is made
Kripya dhyan dein | कृपया ध्यान दें | Attention, please (only to open a joke)
Railway Hindi verbs: gaadi lag gayi (drawn up at the platform), gaadi chhooti, gaadi chali, chart ban gaya, berth mil gayi
'9:40 wali' (a train named by its time)

Railway nouns: gaadi, maal gaadi (goods train), dibba and aakhri dibba (coach, the last coach), patri (track), coach, berth, platform, PNR, chart, waiting list, booking, ticket, checker, running status, board
His past: pitaji (his father, a goods-train guard), colony ka gate, guard
The dal: dal, swaad (taste), ghadi dekhkar (by the clock, which is how it is not made)
Mummy ji, Didi, Bhai sahab, Captain sahab, Masterji (with आप); Tinku (तुम)
never: about, roughly, around, nearly | लगभग, क़रीब, आसपास | lagbhag, kareeb (except quoting the word back in his correction); a script can check his lines for these
sharp, theek, theek-theek as a time word ('theek 6:00'): 'sharp' was worn out by three askers and 'Theek.' is Mausa ji's
'pehle' in the 'X first' sense, or 'pehle se': 'Pehle ___' is yours alone
An English verb with kar or ho: 'confirm ho gaya', 'book kiya', 'note kar liya', 'check karo' (Mummy's frame)
'jaldi karo' or any 'hurry up': he says the minutes left instead
'I missed you', 'I'm proud of you', 'love', or any word about his own feelings
English 'sorry' (Mausi's), 'Galti hui' (Mausa ji's), 'thank you' (Mami's, to strangers), 'Shukriya' and 'Maaf kijiye' (yours)
'Don't worry' (Mama ji's), 'ho jayega' with no time in it, 'pakka'
Other people's words: 'Lo.', 'arre', 'haan?', 'hai na?', 'aur haan', 'Dekhiye', 'Suno', 'not out', 'full', 'Next ball'
Prices or money (Mummy's), scores or cricket words (Tinku's and Captain sahab's), ordinals or numbered items (nobody's in speech)
Two figures in one bubble (the only exception is the Tamil whisper count)
beta, or any word for you that fixes gender (rule 8; rulebook Q7)
A Hindi form that marks your gender: no -ोगे/-ोगी future, no 'pahunch gaye/gayi', no 'thak gaye', no 'kaun jaayega?' (rule 66); questions to you use the subjunctive ('कौन रखे?')
Whether you travel on his pass: the pass rules treat a grown son and a grown daughter differently (rule 8)
A temperament word about anyone: moody, shy, emotional, bossy, lazy
Anything that doubts a report of harassment, of being followed, or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22)
A rule for choosing in his ask; only the goal of the moment, never the number the two tie on (rule 37); a card person's name or a card note's words in any bubble (rule 36)
A joke while he asks (rule 37); a joke at anyone's cost
Any religious word or exclamation (rule 3): no Hai Ram, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Ishwar; in English mode no Gosh, Goodness, Good grief, Thank God
Slang: chill, bro, scene, whatever
A shout bubble, an exclamation mark, or a year on screen (rules 2 and 35)
address: YOU: तुम only in lines that show no gender (rule 66): commands ('सो लो', 'देखो'), 'who should' asks in the subjunctive ('चेकर के लिए टिकट कौन रखे?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो।', 'तुम्हें कभी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।'). Possessives agree with the thing, not you ('बर्थ 36 तुम्हारी है', flagged by check 2 and cleared). No name, no beta, no family word; he often opens with the time instead of 'you'. You answer 'Ji Papa' and आप, exactly as you speak to Mummy.
NANI: 'Mummy ji', आप and -इए ('Mummy ji, aap baithiye.'). She is the one he talks to most and longest, because she lets him finish. Readers confirm the word carries no community lean.
MUMMY: no address word; he opens with the time ('Nau baj gaye.'); both say तुम, so the game's own couple carries no honorific-to-husband pattern.
MAMA JI: to his face तुम and no name (the household has no first names); to you he is 'Mama ji'. Mama ji calls him 'Jija ji'.
MAUSI: 'Didi', आप. MAUSA JI: 'Bhai sahab', आप. Both wait on the Hindi-first and South Indian readers (rule 65) and the one family address table.
MASTERJI and CAPTAIN SAHAB: by their titles, आप.
MAMI: no name, आप (his formality, even to a younger in-law).
A CHILD: commands only ('Gilaas seedha karo.'), so no gender.
STRANGERS AND CARD PEOPLE: आप and 'ji', always; to the ticket checker the count comes first: 'Ji, S4 mein solah hain.' | 'जी, S4 में सोलह हैं।'
samples: GIVING AN ORDER (the lead-in to the 1.08 ask: the headcount, then the goal of the moment; rule 37, both halves of the twin in this same three-bubble shape): 'There are sixteen of us. / We have only twelve berths. / The train leaves at 9:40.' | 'Hum solah log hain. / Berth sirf baarah hain. / Gaadi chhootne ka time 9:40 hai.' | 'हम सोलह लोग हैं। / बर्थ सिर्फ़ बारह हैं। / गाड़ी छूटने का समय 9:40 है।' (One figure a bubble (the old single bubble held four). Count before the noun, his alone. The third bubble is a station announcement's own shape ('gaadi ke chhootne ka samay').)

ANNOUNCING WHAT COMES NEXT (the train pulls in at the junction; the matrix sample, with 'pehle' taken out because 'Pehle ___' is yours): 'The train is in. / Coach S4 is at the front. / The bags go up next.' | 'Gaadi lag gayi hai. / S4 aage hai. / Ab bag upar jaayenge.' | 'गाड़ी लग गई है। / S4 आगे है। / अब बैग ऊपर जाएँगे।' ('Gaadi lagna' (a train drawn up at the platform) is railway Hindi with a Hindi verb.)

GIVING AN ORDER (the bay at night): 'Bags go under the berths. / Lights go out at ten. / The ticket checker comes next.' | 'Bag berth ke neeche jaayenge. / Batti das baje bujhegi. / Ab checker aayega.' | 'बैग बर्थ के नीचे जाएँगे। / बत्ती दस बजे बुझेगी। / अब चेकर आएगा।' (Rule 66 flags जाएँगे, बुझेगी, आएगा (futures); they agree with bags, lights and the checker, not you, so a native reader clears them.)

MOVED (1.10: he lays the list on the lower berth, turned to you, taps it twice and takes his hand away): 'My battery has died. / Tonight, you are in charge.' | 'Meri battery khatam hai. / Aaj raat in-charge tum ho.' | 'मेरी बैटरी ख़त्म है। / आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो।' (Hindi changed from 'ख़त्म हो गई' to 'ख़त्म है' so the line raises no flag at all. You are not the doer of 'इंचार्ज तुम हो'.)

WORRYING (to Mummy on the platform; the refreshing is what kills his battery by ten): 'The train is twelve minutes late. / Now it is fourteen. / I will check the running status again.' | 'Gaadi baarah minute late hai. / Ab chaudah ho gaye. / Running status phir dekhta hoon.' | 'गाड़ी बारह मिनट लेट है। / अब चौदह हो गए। / मैं रनिंग स्टेटस फिर देखता हूँ।' (Said to Mummy, not you.)

TEASING (Mama ji on the phone, who has booked the night before again; 'Kamaal hai.' as dry irony): 'You booked tomorrow's train tonight? / Remarkable.' | 'Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat bana? / Kamaal hai.' | 'कल की गाड़ी का टिकट आज रात बना? / कमाल है।' (No figure. 'Badi himmat hai' goes: the exclamation now carries the irony. 'Book kiya' goes: an English verb with kar is Mummy's frame.)

TEASING (Captain sahab, at the lane ground on cup day): 'Captain sahab, you said nine o'clock. / I have been here since 8:55.' | 'Captain sahab, aapne nau baje kaha tha. / Main 8:55 se khada hoon.' | 'कप्तान साहब, आपने नौ बजे कहा था। / मैं 8:55 से खड़ा हूँ।' (One figure a bubble; the old 'nine o'clock means 8:55' held two.)

PRAISING (the bay at dawn, nobody missing): 'Everyone is on the train. / Nobody was left behind. / It is all confirmed.' | 'Sab log gaadi mein hain. / Koi peeche nahin chhoota. / Sab confirm hai.' | 'सब लोग गाड़ी में हैं। / कोई पीछे नहीं छूटा। / सब कन्फ़र्म है।' (His highest praise, now 'Sab confirm hai.' (the railway status word) in place of 'Confirm ho gaya.' (an English verb with ho, Mummy's frame). No figure. छूटा is flagged and cleared: it agrees with 'koi'.)

PRAISING YOU (the album, in its own panel, never Nani's): 'Four trains this year. / Nobody ever had to remind you.' | 'Is saal chaar trainein huin. / Tumhein kabhi yaad nahin dilana pada.' | 'इस साल चार ट्रेनें हुईं। / तुम्हें कभी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।' ('Ek baar bhi' became 'kabhi' so the second bubble carries no figure. पड़ा is impersonal and हुईं agrees with ट्रेनें; both are flagged and cleared.)
SAYING NO (to Mausi at the station, who wants one more change): 'No, Didi. / The chart is made.' | 'Didi, nahin. / Chart ban chuka hai.' | 'दीदी, नहीं। / चार्ट बन चुका है।' (His final no. No figure.)

COMFORTING (you, after the long halt): 'Nani's house is four hours away. / Sleep for three.' | 'Nani ke ghar tak chaar ghante hain. / Teen ghante so lo.' | 'नानी के घर तक चार घंटे हैं। / तीन घंटे सो लो।' (A command to you: no gender.)

LOSING HIS TEMPER (a two-minute stop, not the long halt; the minutes left, one word twice, the guard's flat hand lowered palm down; the English goes): 'We have two minutes here. / Nobody gets down. / Nobody.' | 'Yahan sirf do minute hain. / Koi neeche na utre. / Koi nahin.' | 'यहाँ सिर्फ़ दो मिनट हैं। / कोई नीचे न उतरे। / कोई नहीं।' ('Halt' goes with the rest of the English when he is cross.)

A JOKE AT HOME (calling everyone to dinner; deadpan, delivered like the station loudspeaker; never while he asks, rule 37; rulebook Q5): 'Attention, please. / The dal has arrived on platform one.' | 'Kripya dhyan dein. / Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.' | 'कृपया ध्यान दें। / दाल प्लेटफ़ॉर्म नंबर एक पर आ चुकी है।' (The announcement frame is his joke shape, at most once a chapter. 'Kripya' is the everyday formal 'please' of every public sign.)

A JOKE ABOUT HIMSELF (kept from his file): 'I was born at 6:10. / On time, my mother said.' | 'Main 6:10 par paida hua. / Maa kehti thin, time par.' | 'मैं 6:10 पर पैदा हुआ। / माँ कहती थीं, टाइम पर।' (About himself, at nobody's cost.)

THE DAL (Tinku asks how long it takes; the one thing he will not time): 'Dal is not made by the clock. / It is made by taste.' | 'Dal ghadi dekhkar nahin banti. / Swaad se banti hai.' | 'दाल घड़ी देखकर नहीं बनती। / स्वाद से बनती है।' (His one interest with no number in it (comics review: give Papa an interest on the page that is not a number). Said plainly, never praised by anyone (india review).)

CARE, WITH MAUSI (the 1.13 lead-in, after her 'Lower berth for me, obviously'; the deed done ahead, said as a fact): 'Didi, the lower berth is yours. / It was done in March.' | 'Didi, neeche ki berth aapki hai. / March mein hi ho gayi thi.' | 'दीदी, नीचे की बर्थ आपकी है। / मार्च में ही हो गई थी।' (Replaces 'lower berth 33 is already yours': no figure, and no 'pehle se'.)

THANKING NANI (dawn at her gate, the tea already poured on her step): 'Mummy ji, the tea was on the step at 5:52. / Noted.' | 'Mummy ji, 5:52 par chai seedhi par thi. / Darj hai.' | 'मम्मी जी, 5:52 पर चाय सीढ़ी पर थी। / दर्ज है।' (His thanks: the deed and its minute, then 'Darj hai.' (entered in the register).)

WITH NANI, THE LONGEST RUN (she is the one who lets him finish; facts of his past, the feeling left under them; proposed for the dawn at her gate or the album, never on the wordless 2:10 halt panel, which stays silent): 'My father was a goods-train guard. / His train was often late. / I waited at the colony gate.' | 'Mere pitaji maal gaadi ke guard the. / Unki gaadi aksar der se aati thi. / Main colony ke gate par khada rehta tha.' | 'मेरे पिताजी मालगाड़ी के गार्ड थे। / उनकी गाड़ी अक्सर देर से आती थी। / मैं कॉलोनी के गेट पर खड़ा रहता था।' (No figure in three bubbles. He states what happened and never says how it felt, so his contradiction holds. Optional: the owner may keep the boy wordless only.)

SAYING SORRY (shown wrong in front of the family: the record against himself): '9:40 was my time. / It was wrong. / The board says 9:25.' | '9:40 mera time tha. / Galat nikla. / Board par 9:25 hai.' | '9:40 मेरा टाइम था। / ग़लत निकला। / बोर्ड पर 9:25 है।' (Never 'sorry' (Mausi's) and never 'Galti hui' (Mausa ji's).)

THE OPENING (proposed 1.04, the kitchen, the dal pot behind him painted without comment): 'Booking for May opens in March. / My alarm is set.' | 'May ki booking March mein khulegi. / Alarm lag gaya hai.' | 'मई की बुकिंग मार्च में खुलेगी। / अलार्म लग गया है।' (Kept from his file (the 60-day window). खुलेगी and गया है agree with the booking and the alarm.)

COUNTING THE COACHES IN (a whisper to himself before 1.08; Tamil in every mode; a Tamil reader signs it off): '...naalu, anju, aaru.' | '...naalu, anju, aaru.' | '...नालु, अंजु, आरु।' (Tamil script நாலு, அஞ்சு, ஆறு (four, five, six). The one marked exception to one figure a bubble: a whisper with no listener, once in chapter 1.)

habits: DEVICE: a plain black smartphone in a plain black case, in his trouser pocket, charged every night at ten; normal text size, since his eyes are good. On the night train it dies by 10 pm because he has refreshed the running status since noon (the worry line's reason, shown plainly, never as an age joke).

SCRIPT: English in Latin letters for everything he types, in all three language modes, because that is how he types and because 'Reached?' marks no gender while 'पहुँच गए?' does (rule 66). Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages too.

SHAPE: he types the way he speaks. Each line is one short whole English sentence with its verb, a capital and a full stop, one fact to a line, in order. Times in figures with a colon (9:40, never 9.40 or 'nine forty').

NUMBERS: the speech budget carried onto the screen: at most one figure a line, and at least one line in three with none ('Charge your phone tonight.'). No prices, no scores, no numbered lists (no '1.', no ticks: Mami's), no ordinals.

THREE FIXED LINES, his only ones with no full sentence: 'Reached?' (after any journey you make without him; it means 'I missed you'; his alone in the cast), 'Noted.' (his reply when he has nothing to add), 'Good morning.' (under the 6:35 picture).

FULL STOPS: the family reads them as cross; they are not. The method notes cite NPR's report of a study where a one-word text ending in a full stop read as less sincere. The story can use the misreading once, with Tinku explaining it.
SPEED: one slow forefinger, the phone in his other palm; he rereads before sending; no typos; autocorrect off.

REPLIES: within a minute, always ('Noted.'), distinct from Mausa ji's 'Ok.' an hour later. Distinct too from Captain sahab's telegram style with no punctuation, Mummy's and Tinku's lowercase, and Mama ji's and Mausi's doubled marks.
EMOJI AND STICKERS: none. VOICE NOTES: never sends one (he says they have no time in them); he listens to Mausi's in full and replies in text.

FORWARDS: none, except one good-morning picture to the family at 6:35, after the walk with Captain sahab (a sunflower, or a glass of tea on a sunny windowsill; never a lotus, which is a party symbol, never a marigold, which leans to ritual, never a god or a famous face, rule 3) with 'Good morning.' under it. Never politics, never false news, never a forward he has not read.
CALLS: anything that matters is a call, made at the minute he said he would call. Nani gets calls, never texts.
TIMING: 'Reached?' goes out within ten minutes of your train's due time, by the running status, not the timetable.
ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' label, no group chat (owner, 23 Oct).
samples: TO YOU, MARCH, BOOKING DAY: 'The booking is done. / We have 12 berths. / They are on my railway pass and 2 PNRs.' then, a month later, on its own: 'Mausi has added 4 names. / No berths are left.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'बुकिंग हो गई। / हमारे पास 12 बर्थ हैं। / मेरे रेलवे पास और 2 PNR पर हैं।' then 'मौसी ने 4 नाम और जोड़े। / अब कोई बर्थ नहीं बची।' (who is on the pass is never said, rule 8; 'railway pass' because 'मेरे पास' alone also means 'with me')

TO YOU, THE NIGHT BEFORE: 'We are in coach S4. / Berth 36 is yours, a lower berth. / The train comes on platform 3. / It leaves at 9:40. / Carry your own water bottle. / Charge your phone tonight.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'हम कोच S4 में हैं। / बर्थ 36 तुम्हारी है, नीचे की। / गाड़ी प्लेटफ़ॉर्म 3 पर आती है। / 9:40 पर छूटती है। / पानी की बोतल अपनी रखना। / आज रात बैटरी पूरी रखना।' (four lines with one figure, two with none; 36 is a real lower berth in the run 33 to 44, so Mausi keeps 33; the last line is the irony nobody remarks on: by ten that night his own phone is dead)
TO YOU, AFTER ANY JOURNEY WITHOUT HIM: 'Reached?' (one word, in English letters in every mode)
TO YOU, AFTER THE WARD NIGHT, 10:02 AM: 'Nani reached home at 10:00. / Sleep now.' | 'नानी 10:00 बजे घर पहुँच गईं। / अब सो लो।'
TO YOU, A WEEKDAY, WHEN YOU WILL BE HOME LATE (his one message with no number and nothing to arrange): 'The dal is on the stove.' | 'दाल गैस पर है।'
REPLY TO ANYTHING YOU SEND: 'Noted.' | 'दर्ज है।'

TO MAMI, DECEMBER: 'The guest train times are below. / The morning train is at 6:10. / The night train is at 9:40. / Both are confirmed. / I will meet both.' | 'मेहमानों की गाड़ियों का समय नीचे है। / सुबह की गाड़ी 6:10 पर है। / रात की गाड़ी 9:40 पर है। / दोनों कन्फ़र्म हैं। / दोनों पर मैं रहूँगा।' (she answers with her own list; his name heads her item 1 'Papa: trains', in her shape, not his)

THE FAMILY, EVERY MORNING (mentioned, never shown as a group; if a message is ever shown it is one message card with no group name, app look or 'forwarded' label): a picture of a sunflower at 6:35, then 'Good morning.'

test_lines.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner.
test_lines.en: Remarkable. Tonight even the power went on time.
test_lines.hinglish: Kamaal hai. Aaj bijli bhi time par gayi.
test_lines.hi: कमाल है। आज बिजली भी टाइम पर गई।

test_lines.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late. (to Mama ji, the latecomer; cross: the minutes, then one word twice; the English goes, so 'late' becomes 'der')
test_lines.en: You are 120 minutes late. Dinner is cold. Cold.
test_lines.hinglish: Tum 120 minute der se aaye. Khana thanda hai. Thanda.
test_lines.hi: तुम 120 मिनट देर से आए। खाना ठंडा है। ठंडा।

test_lines.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job. (to the cousin; no verb agrees with the cousin)
test_lines.en: So it is confirmed. I will find your joining-day train.
test_lines.hinglish: Sab confirm hai. Joining ki gaadi main dekh leta hoon.
test_lines.hi: सब कन्फ़र्म है। जॉइनिंग की गाड़ी मैं देख लेता हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it. (to Tinku, who made it; the polite no is the joke)
test_lines.en: Attention, please. This sugar also contains some tea.
test_lines.hinglish: Kripya dhyan dein. Is cheeni mein chai bhi hai.
test_lines.hi: कृपया ध्यान दें। इस चीनी में चाय भी है।

test_lines.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong. (he is the one who was wrong)
test_lines.en: 9:40 was my time. It was wrong. The board's right.
test_lines.hinglish: 9:40 mera time tha. Galat nikla. Board sahi hai.
test_lines.hi: 9:40 मेरा टाइम था। ग़लत निकला। बोर्ड सही है।

test_lines.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform. (to you, as the train starts)
test_lines.en: The 7:25 is moving. I stay till the last coach.
test_lines.hinglish: 7:25 wali chal padi. Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.
test_lines.hi: 7:25 वाली चल पड़ी। आख़िरी डिब्बे तक मैं यहीं हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did.
test_lines.en: Noted. The return tickets come next.
test_lines.hinglish: Darj hai. Ab wapsi ka ticket aayega.
test_lines.hi: दर्ज है। अब वापसी का टिकट आएगा।

test_lines.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing. (to Captain sahab, who brought it)
test_lines.en: What time does it shut? Without one, it isn't news.
test_lines.hinglish: Kitne baje band hogi? Bina time ke khabar nahin banti.
test_lines.hi: कितने बजे बंद होगी? बिना टाइम के ख़बर नहीं बनती।

test_lines.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house.
test_lines.en: The tracks will flood too. I will check the 8:15.
test_lines.hinglish: Patri par bhi paani hoga. 8:15 wali gaadi dekhta hoon.
test_lines.hi: पटरी पर भी पानी होगा। 8:15 वाली गाड़ी देखता हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 10. Someone asks them how they are.
test_lines.en: Every train is on time. So I am too.
test_lines.hinglish: Sab gaadiyan time par hain. Matlab main bhi.
test_lines.hi: सब गाड़ियाँ टाइम पर हैं। मतलब मैं भी।

test_lines.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table. (to the child; commands only, so no gender)
test_lines.en: Never mind. Stand the glass up. The cloth comes next.
test_lines.hinglish: Koi baat nahin. Gilaas seedha karo. Ab kapda aayega.
test_lines.hi: कोई बात नहीं। गिलास सीधा करो। अब कपड़ा आएगा।

test_lines.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news.
test_lines.en: Remarkable. The news came at 11:52. I have noted it.
test_lines.hinglish: Kamaal hai. Khabar 11:52 par aayi. Darj kar li.
test_lines.hi: कमाल है। ख़बर 11:52 पर आई। दर्ज कर ली।

changed: LENGTH (C2): from one sentence of four to ten words a beat, which put him among the eight clipped speakers, to an ordered run of whole sentences across one to three bubbles, each one fact, the last naming the next step. He is now one of the four long talkers, and his long shape (closed announcements in order) is unlike Mama ji's run-on, Mausi's triple and Masterji's wander.

NUMBERS (C1): kept as one of the two leaners, because the timetable is his essence, but budgeted at one figure a bubble and one bubble in three with none. The 1.08 line 'Sixteen of us have twelve berths. 9:40, not 9:45.' held four figures in one bubble; it is now three bubbles of one figure each. Five of his twelve test lines carry a figure. Prices, scores and ordinals are out of his speech and his card notes ('a fourth time' became 'again').

THE QUOTED LINE: '9:40, not 9:45.' became '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, not "around".' It keeps the correction and moves his quarrel to where his never list already put it (vague times), with one figure. Owner call: the old line was picked by the players' judge, so it may stay as one marked two-figure exception if the owner prefers it.

EXCLAMATION (C6): none before; now 'Kamaal hai.' | 'Remarkable.', said flat with a full stop, for real surprise and for dry irony. No religious sense. Mama ji's 'Kamaal!' goes so the word has one owner.

SORRY (C4): never in words before; now the record corrected against himself: '9:40 mera time tha. Galat nikla.' plus the right fact. Kept apart from Mausa ji's 'Galti hui.' (no subject, no time) and Mausi's 'sorry'.

THANKS (C4): before, only the praise 'It's confirmed.'; now the deed and its minute, then 'Darj hai.' (entered in the register), and the same word when he is thanked, followed by the next job. 'Darj' is Hindi and is the parcel register's word, so his English stays railway nouns and times only.

MIX (C12): 'Confirm ho gaya.' and 'note kar liya' were an English word plus ho or kar, the frame the matrix gives to Mummy alone. They became 'Sab confirm hai.' (the railway status) and 'Darj hai.'; his verbs are now Hindi railway verbs (gaadi lagna, chhootna, chalna, chart banna). When cross even 'late' and 'halt' go.

WORDS FROM (C11): beyond railway nouns, now his own past (his father the goods-train guard, the colony gate, the last coach, 'the 9:40 wali') and the dal he cooks by taste, his one interest with no number ('Dal ghadi dekhkar nahin banti. Swaad se banti hai.'), as the comics review asked for Papa, Mummy and Mami.

FEELING (C3): still a deed and never a feeling word, but the deed is now spoken as something already done ahead ('Neeche ki berth aapki hai. March mein hi ho gayi thi.'), which tells him apart from Mausa ji's deed with his hands, now, and from Mummy's shop news. The colony-gate boy gets one spoken run, to Nani only, as facts with the feeling left under them; it is optional and never on the wordless 2:10 halt panel.

HOW ARE YOU (C10): he no longer dodges with a clock time; he answers with the state of everyone's trains ('Sab gaadiyan time par hain. Matlab main bhi.'), no figure, which also says what he wants: everyone arriving.

HUMOUR (C13): still deadpan about himself and clocks, now with a frame of its own, the station loudspeaker ('Kripya dhyan dein. Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.'), so his dry lines cannot be mistaken for Captain sahab's sardonic calls or your deadpan mirror. At most once a chapter, never while he asks, and all of it waits on rulebook Q5.

ONE OWNER PER WORD (matrix 2.15): dropped 'sharp' and 'theek' (worn out by three askers; 'Theek.' is Mausa ji's), 'pehle' and 'pehle se' (yours: 'Lower berth 33 is already yours' and 'Bag pehle upar' were rewritten), 'pakka', and 'Badi himmat hai' (the irony now rides on 'Kamaal hai.').

TALKS TO (C15): his longest runs go to Nani, who lets him finish; test lines are also said to Mama ji (the latecomer), the cousin, Tinku (the sugar), Captain sahab (the rumour) and a child, so he is heard with others, not only with you.

RULE 66: Hindi lines to you were reworded where it cost nothing ('बैटरी ख़त्म है' for 'ख़त्म हो गई', 'छूटने का समय 9:40 है' for a future), and the album's 'एक बार भी' became 'कभी'. The checker will still flag lines such as बुझेगी, जाएँगे, आएगा, छूटा, पड़ा, हुईं, चली, यहीं हूँ and तुम्हारी है; each agrees with a thing, 'koi', an adverb or Papa himself, never with you, and a native reader clears them.

TYPING: one figure a line and at least one line in three with none (the old night-before message had 'Berths 33 to 44' and 'Platform 3. 9:40.' on single lines); each line a whole English sentence with its verb, the way he speaks; added the dal message, his one text with no number; your berth is 36, a real lower berth in the 33 to 44 run, so Mausi keeps 33; 'my railway pass' so the Hindi 'मेरे पास' cannot be read as 'with me'. 'Reached?', 'Noted.', the 6:35 sunflower, no emoji and no voice notes all stay.

KEPT AS THEY WERE: essence, want, fear and contradiction; 'Tonight, you are in charge.' at 1.10 with the list laid on the berth; the booking line at 1.04; the 6:10 birth joke; 'Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai.'; the Tamil count (now the one marked exception to one figure a bubble, a whisper to himself, once in chapter 1); the cross tell (minutes left, one word twice, the guard's flat hand); every address word and every rule-66 form to you.
